title: Mandu on 23 November 1305
subtitle: The Last Echo of the Paramaras
era: Delhi Sultanate conquest of Malwa, 1305-1310 CE
region: Mandu, Dhar, Ujjain, Chanderi, and the last Paramara corner of Malwa
moral: A dynasty can fall, yet still leave a last voice in stone.

sources.citation: Amir Khusrau, Khazain-ul-Futuh, trans. Mohammad Habib; Elliot and Dowson, History of India as Told by Its Own Historians Vol. III
sources.note: Primary Persian account of the 1305 conquest, read as court panegyric.

sources.citation: Udaipur, Madhya Pradesh inscription of 1310 CE; H.V. Trivedi, CII Vol. VII
sources.note: Last epigraphic survival of Paramara authority after Mandu's fall.

sources.citation: Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (2003), pp. 198-199; B.P. Saksena in HCIP Vol. VI (1992)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of Alauddin Khalji's Malwa campaign.

panels.shot: wide, looming three-quarter view of Mandu fort on its plateau at dusk, with Alauddin Khalji's army encamped below and Mahalakadeva and Goga silhouetted on the ramparts

dialogue.text: On 23 November 1305, as Mandu’s heights braced for assault, a broken kingdom, a minister called Goga, and a king named Mahalakadeva faced Alauddin Khalji’s general—and left one last voice in stone.

panels.shot: slow push-in over a tattered royal parasol lying in dust beside a cracked temple wall at Dhar

dialogue.text: By the early fourteenth century, the Paramara kingdom of Malwa was a shadow of its age under Raja Bhoja. Dhar still held a throne, but its reach had shrunk and its rivals had grown.

panels.shot: medium interior shot in Dhar court, slightly high angle, emphasizing the pressure on the throne and the prominence of Goga beside it

dialogue.text: Mahalakadeva sat on Bhoja’s old throne, but command in the field had passed to his minister, Goga. Persian chroniclers would call him Koka and remember him as the real defender of Malwa.

panels.shot: map-like bird’s-eye view over central India with stylized arrows from Delhi towards Malwa, fading into a real landscape of marching troops

dialogue.text: From Delhi, Alauddin Khalji turned his eye to Malwa. After Gujarat and Ranthambhor, he sent Ayn al-Mulk Multani to break this last independent corner, tighten his ring of power, and seize its wealth.

panels.shot: dynamic low-angle shot of Ayn al-Mulk Multani’s vanguard cresting a ridge, but his face unseen, focusing on armor and banners

dialogue.text: Amir Khusrau, in his Khazain-ul-Futuh, sings of Multani’s march, claiming vast hosts and countless foes. His words are court praise, but they mark a real campaign of steel, calculation, and siege.

panels.shot: tight two-shot of Mahalakadeva and Goga in council, lamplight carving their faces, with a map of Malwa between them

dialogue.speaker: Goga
dialogue.text: If we hold Mandu and break their first rush, Malwa still has breath.

panels.shot: wide shot of Mandu plateau seen from below, with defenders on ramparts and Goga riding along the walls

dialogue.text: Mandu became their shield. On that rugged plateau, Goga gathered what he could—the remnants of Paramara forces, hill-men, city guards—and braced for Multani’s onset.

panels.shot: chaotic mid-range battle scene outside Mandu, focusing on Goga’s contingent clashing with advancing Delhi cavalry

dialogue.text: Amir Khusrau describes fierce fighting before Mandu. He praises Multani’s charge and tells of Goga’s resistance, of lines breaking and reforming in the dust and cries at the foot of the hill.

panels.shot: somber medium shot of Goga captured, hands bound, kneeling; Mahalakadeva glimpsed far away on the walls as a tiny figure

dialogue.text: In the struggle outside, Goga fell into the hands of Multani’s men. Court chroniclers do not dwell on his words at capture. They dwell on what his fate was made to say.

panels.shot: grim close-up of a covered bundle on a cart leaving the battlefield, soldiers around; camera angle from behind, destination unseen

dialogue.text: Amir Khusrau records that Goga’s head was severed and sent to Delhi. In the panegyric, it becomes a trophy of obedience and terror, a warning carried across the plains to Alauddin’s court.

panels.shot: wide shot inside a lofty hall in Delhi, low angle on Alauddin’s throne with a distant tray presented below, faces of courtiers half-lit

dialogue.text: In Delhi, the arrival of Goga’s head was made spectacle. Chroniclers describe it to magnify Alauddin’s might and the fall of Malwa’s minister, a courtly ritual of victory and humiliation.

panels.shot: majestic mid-shot of the Dhar iron pillar standing in a courtyard, viewed slightly from below to emphasize its height and antiquity

dialogue.text: With Goga gone, Multani moved on Dhar, the Paramara capital. Amir Khusrau notes the breaking of the great iron pillar there—an ancient emblem of the dynasty’s endurance and pride.

panels.shot: dynamic close shot of Delhi soldiers heaving ropes around the iron pillar, the moment before it cracks, faces strained

dialogue.text: Khusrau boasts how the Dhar pillar was cast down. His verse presents it as the fall of Paramara strength itself, a sign that their line, once towering, now lay toppled in the dust.

panels.shot: sunset wide shot of Mandu fort again, this time ringed by siege works, towers and trenches, tents closer and more numerous

dialogue.text: Yet Mandu still held. As Multani’s men tightened the siege, Mandu’s cliffs and walls turned days into weeks of stalemate. The question now was not attack—but entry.

panels.shot: tense interior shot in a dim Mandu passageway, with a shadowed figure leading Delhi soldiers toward a narrow gate from inside

dialogue.text: Sources speak of betrayal—a secret entrance shown to the besiegers. On 23 November 1305, Multani’s men slipped through a hidden way, turning Mandu’s height from shield into trap.

panels.shot: urgent medium shot of Mahalakadeva inside Mandu, armor hastily donned, as news of the breach reaches him

dialogue.speaker: Mahalakadeva and Goga
dialogue.text: If the walls fail, we stand by the springs that fed our fathers.

panels.shot: somber wide shot near a rocky spring within Mandu, with Mahalakadeva’s small force facing advancing Delhi troops among rocks and trees

dialogue.text: Tradition in the chronicles says Mahalakadeva was killed near a spring. There, in that last stand within his own fortress, the direct line of Paramara kings ended in close-pressed combat.

panels.shot: quiet aftermath shot inside Mandu: abandoned weapons and a deserted courtyard, smoke haze softening the scene

dialogue.text: After Mandu’s fall, Malwa passed under Delhi’s control. Amir Khusrau exults in the conquest, swelling numbers and victories, but behind his verses lie emptied courtyards and silenced councils.

panels.shot: transition shot from a carved Paramara emblem fading into Alauddin-era administrative figures distributing orders over Malwa

dialogue.text: Within years, Delhi’s governors and tax-collectors settled into Malwa’s cities. Castles, markets, and temples that once answered to Dhar now answered to the Khalji sultanate’s officers.

panels.shot: serene close-up of the 1310 Udaipur inscription on a stone slab, sunlight grazing the carved letters, surroundings slightly blurred

dialogue.text: Yet in 1310, a stone at Udaipur in Madhya Pradesh still bore a Paramara grant. H.V. Trivedi published its text—a faint, final assertion of authority carved five years after Mandu’s capture.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot of Mandu’s ruins at sunrise, with distant figures of modern visitors walking among them

dialogue.text: Mahalakadeva, Goga, Ayn al-Mulk, and Alauddin are gone; their choices remain in forts, broken pillars, and one last inscription. A dynasty ended, but its history still speaks, if we listen to the stone.
